A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same selective-SSM generalization research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite substantial restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original training/test accuracies and generalization-gap results on synthetic majority classification and IMDb sentiment classification.

after.justification: v2 retains the classification results and adds original training-loss and spectral-abscissa trajectories for models initialized in an unstable regime.

M1.justification: The selective-SSM recurrence, input projections, softplus step size, discretization, and embedding/single-block/readout architecture remain unchanged. The regularization cited in v2 was already used in v1. Broader theoretical assumptions and experimental initializations do not introduce a new method.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same binary majority task and IMDb sentiment task. Sparse Majority is renamed Majority, while its generation and noise procedure remain unchanged. The added stability experiments reuse these tasks; their differences concern model initialization and evaluation procedure.

E2.justification: Neither version empirically evaluates competing methods against the selective SSM. v2's new Table 1 compares theoretical bounds for different architectures, rather than adding experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds a distinct early-training protocol: unstable initialization with sA = 0.1, 10 epochs, and 10% of each dataset balanced across labels. It tracks stability and training loss across sequence lengths, substantially extending v1's evaluation focused on generalization after training.

E4.justification: v2's Experiment 1 and Figure 1 add a substantial stability analysis asking whether training can stabilize initially unstable models as sequence length increases. Both tasks receive spectral-abscissa and loss trajectories. v1 examined generalization across lengths but did not investigate these training-failure dynamics.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed information, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars. The new trajectories do not introduce uncertainty-reporting procedures.

E6.justification: v2 adds spectral-abscissa and training-loss results showing stabilization and loss reduction for shorter sequences, versus persistent instability and very large losses for longer sequences under the new protocol. The earlier accuracy-versus-length curves are retained in Figure 2; no same-setting performance improvement is established.

T1.justification: v1's separate stable fixed-step and input-dependent-step bounds are replaced by Theorem 3.3's broader spectral-abscissa analysis, with revised assumptions and finite-length expressions. v2 also introduces linear-attention Proposition 3.4 and Rademacher-complexity lower bounds in Theorem 4.1, with substantial proof revisions and new proofs in Appendices D–F.

C1.justification: The headline contributions broaden from length-independent generalization under stability assumptions to claims about stable and unstable regimes, a formal linear-attention bound, and failure to stabilize long-sequence training. These claims reshape the abstract, contribution statements, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting training failure to instability and proposing an implicit bias toward the stability boundary to preserve long-range information. It expands comparisons involving softmax normalization and bounded RNN activations, and acknowledges an O(T) gap between its upper and lower complexity bounds.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link and documents initialization and training-budget details. In particular, sA = 0 is newly disclosed for the retained generalization experiment, without establishing an initialization change. The documented N = 4, d = 16 architecture and dataset-processing details remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 replaces much of the historical survey with recent SSM expressivity and generalization research, including Sarrof, Nandakumar, and Terzic and colleagues. Section 4 and Table 1 substantially expand the positioning against attention, RNN, and LTI-SSM bounds through explicit comparisons of assumptions and scaling.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, contributions, analysis, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work is integrated into the introduction, model preliminaries are consolidated, analysis becomes a separate section, and Rademacher-complexity background moves to Appendix D.

P2.justification: The two-column main text becomes single-column. v2 adds the bound-comparison table and four-panel stability figure, combines the retained accuracy plots into Figure 2, and removes their separate generalization-gap panels. Appendix histograms and the unchanged IMDb summary table are resized or relocated.

improvement.justification: The new experiments and code link are useful, but v2 introduces errors affecting its central theoretical extensions. Unlike v1's stable-system argument, Lemma D.3, Eq. 53, substitutes a lower step-size bound into an increasing exponential when sA > 0, invalidating the claimed upper bound for that regime. Theorem 4.1's arbitrary-dataset lower bound is also contradicted by zero-input datasets; Appendix F analyzes only constant-one inputs. These defects undermine the expanded headline guarantees and outweigh the added empirical and explanatory material.
